samples.summary: `stripConfigDirectives()` can be made to SYNTHESIZE a live `%%{init:...}%%` directive: a single-pass global `String.replace` lets the residue on either side of a removed match concatenate into a fresh carrier, defeating layer 2 entirely
samples.evidence:
`stripConfigDirectives` (mermaid.ts:227) is `source.replace(FRONTMATTER_RE,'').replace(DIRECTIVE_RE,'')` — one non-iterated pass. `String.replace` with /g stitches the unmatched gaps back together, and the gaps can themselves form a directive.

PoC fence body:
```mermaid
%%%{a}%%%{init: {"dompurifyConfig": {...}} }%%
flowchart LR
  A-->B
```
Trace of DIRECTIVE_RE = /%{2}{\s*(?:(\w+)\s*:|(\w+))\s*(?:(\w+)|((?:(?!}%{2}).|\r?\n)*))?\s*(?:}%{2})?/gi over `%%%{a}%%%{init: … }%%`:
- index 0: `%%` then char2=`%` != `{` -> no match.
- index 1: `%%`(1,2) + `{`(3) -> matches; `(\w+)`=`a`; the optional body branch matches empty (the `(?!}%{2})` lookahead fires on `}%%`); `(?:}%{2})?` consumes `}%%` at 5-7. Match = chars 1..7 = "%%{a}%%". lastIndex = 8.
- from index 8 the remainder is `%{init: … }%%` — only ONE leading `%`, so `%{2}{` never matches again.
Result = char0 (`%`) + chars8.. (`%{init: … }%%`) = `%%{init: {"dompurifyConfig": {...}} }%%` — a syntactically valid directive that is then handed to `mermaid.render(id, stripConfigDirectives(source))` at mermaid.ts:468. Mermaid re-runs its own `detectInit` on the string we pass it, finds the reconstructed directive, and merges it into the process-global config.

Attacker: any workspace collaborator or editor-role share-link visitor writes that fence; it renders in every other viewer's session (`packages/frontend/src/app/shared/shared-document.tsx:315` mounts NotesView for share links, so this is cross-account). Only mermaid's own `secure` key list stands between the restored directive and the config — which is exactly the layer this module's own doc comment (mermaid.ts:29-33) declares insufficient. See my separate finding on `dompurifyConfig` for what a restored directive reaches.

Fix shape: loop the replace to a fixed point, or split/scan rather than a single `replace`.

samples.summary: `SECURE_KEYS` omits `dompurifyConfig`, the one mermaid config key that disables mermaid's OWN label sanitizer — so the stated second line of defence does not pin the most dangerous key
samples.evidence:
SECURE_KEYS (mermaid.ts:167-184) pins `securityLevel`, the theming keys and `htmlLabels`, but not `dompurifyConfig`. Mermaid's `sanitizeText()` honours `config.dompurifyConfig` verbatim when set (`DOMPurify.sanitize(text, config.dompurifyConfig)`), so a directive carrying e.g. `{"dompurifyConfig":{"ALLOWED_TAGS":["img"],"ALLOWED_ATTR":["src","onerror"]}}` relaxes the sanitizer mermaid applies to note-authored label text — text that is inserted into the live `document.body` layout host BEFORE `sanitizeSvg()` ever runs (mermaid.ts:468/484, and the file's own SECURITY note at lines 43-46 confirms this ordering). An `onerror` handler inserted via innerHTML executes; layer 3 only governs what persists afterwards.

This is only reachable if a directive survives layer 2 — which my `stripConfigDirectives` concatenation finding shows it can. The module's design explicitly treats the `secure` list as the backstop for "anything the strip misses" (mermaid.ts:29-33), and the backstop has a hole exactly where it matters. Other unpinned config-reachable knobs in the same class: `wrap`, `deterministicIds`, per-diagram `*.htmlLabels` if mermaid's `sanitize()` does not recurse.

I could not run the engine to confirm the full chain end-to-end (node_modules is not installed in this checkout), hence medium confidence on exploitability; the omission itself is verifiable from the listed constant.

samples.summary: Engine output is laid out in the reader's LIVE `document.body` before `sanitizeSvg()` sees it, so layer 3 cannot stop script execution — `securityLevel:'sandbox'` (upstream's advice for untrusted input) was declined for untrusted, multi-writer content
samples.evidence:
`await mermaid.render(id, ...)` (mermaid.ts:468) runs outside sandbox mode. Mermaid appends a `d<id>` host div to `document.body` and lays the diagram out there (the cleanup at mermaid.ts:484 exists precisely because that host is real and live), so any markup mermaid builds from note text is attached to the reader's document and its side effects (e.g. `onerror`/`onload` on an element inserted via innerHTML into a `<foreignObject>` label) fire before the local DOMPurify pass at mermaid.ts:469 runs. `sanitizeSvg()` therefore only controls what PERSISTS, never what EXECUTES.

Attacker: a collaborator/editor-role share-link visitor authors the fence; it renders in another account's session (`packages/frontend/src/app/shared/shared-document.tsx:315`). There is no application CSP to fall back on — I grepped for `Content-Security-Policy`/`helmet`/`contentSecurityPolicy` and the only hits are inside `.trusted/scripts/agent/node_modules`, none in `packages/backend` or `packages/frontend`.

samples.summary: `CSS_EXTERNAL_RE` only rejects CSS that FETCHES; note-derived, document-scoped CSS that merely restyles the page (UI redress / defacement / clickjacking overlay) passes the `<style>` check untouched
samples.evidence:
`sanitizeSvg()` (mermaid.ts:321-337) keeps any `<style>` whose text does not match `@import|(image-set|image|src|cross-fade)\s*\(|url\(\s*['\"]?\s*(?!#)`. An inline-SVG `<style>` inserted by `apply()` (mermaid.ts:499) is DOCUMENT-scoped — its rules apply to the whole app, not just the preview pane. A payload such as `#root header{display:none}` or `*{position:fixed;top:0;left:0;opacity:0}` contains no fetch construct, so `isSafeCss()` returns true and it is inserted into the reader's page verbatim, enabling UI-redress/phishing overlays over another user's session.

The comment at mermaid.ts:313-317 states the block is dropped whole because "nothing legitimate needs the constructs being rejected" — but the rejection set is fetch-only, not breakout-only. Reachability requires note-controlled text to land in the emitted `<style>` (via `themeCSS`/`themeVariables`/nested font keys), which layer 2 is supposed to prevent and which my `stripConfigDirectives` finding shows is bypassable. Low confidence because I could not run the engine to confirm a concrete key whose value reaches the emitted stylesheet unescaped; the sanitizer gap itself is directly readable at mermaid.ts:275.

samples.summary: `ADD_TAGS: ['use']` re-enables an element DOMPurify excludes by default, and `ALLOWED_URI_REGEXP` lets it point off-page — the comment's claim that references are limited to `#`/`http(s)`/`mailto` is not what the regexp enforces
samples.evidence:
mermaid.ts:241 adds `use` back to the allowlist, and mermaid.ts:264-265 permits any value matching `/^(?:(?:https?|mailto):|[^a-z]|[a-z+.\-]+(?:[^a-z+.\-:]|$))/i`. That regexp allows `https://evil.example/x.svg#a` via the first branch and `//evil.example/x.svg#a` (protocol-relative) plus `/anything` via the `[^a-z]` branch — so `<use href="//evil.example/x.svg#a">` and `<use xlink:href="https://…">` survive sanitization. The comment at mermaid.ts:251-254 asserts the diagram "links out (http(s), mailto:) or within itself (#…), and nothing else"; relative and protocol-relative URLs are a third case that is silently permitted.

Impact is an off-origin reference / IP-logging beacon rather than script execution, and modern browsers restrict cross-origin `<use>` document references, which is why this is minor rather than major. Hardening: keep `use` but constrain its href/xlink:href to `^#`, since mermaid only ever self-references markers and icons.

samples.summary: Diagram-generated `<a target="_blank">` survives sanitization without `rel="noopener noreferrer"` — the preview adds it for markdown links but not for mermaid output (reverse tabnabbing)
samples.evidence: `preview.ts:106-115` deliberately forces `target="_blank"` + `rel="noopener noreferrer"` on markdown links so "the new page" never gets a `window.opener` back into the note. `sanitizeSvg()` applies no such rule: DOMPurify's html profile allows `target`, and `FORBID_ATTR` (mermaid.ts:250) lists only fetch carriers. A mermaid `click A "https://evil.example" _blank` directive (allowed in strict mode — only JS callbacks are blocked; the URL goes through `@braintree/sanitize-url`) therefore produces an `<a href="https://evil.example" target="_blank">` in another user's page with a live `window.opener`. Same class of bug the preview already fixed for markdown links, missed for the new markup path. Fix: add `rel` to the sanitizer hook, or forbid `target`.

samples.summary: With the HTML profile enabled for `<foreignObject>` label subtrees, `FORBID_TAGS` blocks `input` but leaves `form`, `button`, `select`, `textarea`, `label` allowed inside note-derived markup
samples.evidence: mermaid.ts:233 enables `USE_PROFILES: { html: true }` and mermaid.ts:241 re-adds `foreignobject`, so DOMPurify's HTML tag allowlist governs label subtrees. `FORBID_TAGS` (mermaid.ts:249) removes `input` but not `form`/`button`/`select`/`textarea`, so a surviving `<form action="https://evil.example"><button>Sign in</button></form>` inside a diagram label would render as clickable, credential-phishing chrome inside another user's note preview. Mermaid never emits form controls, so forbidding them costs nothing; low confidence because getting arbitrary form markup past mermaid's own strict-mode label sanitizer is not demonstrated.

finding.summary: stripConfigDirectives() can be defeated by directive re-composition: removing one `%%{…}%%` match splices a surviving `%` onto a following `%{init:…}%%`, producing a live directive mermaid will read
finding.evidence:
`stripConfigDirectives` (mermaid.ts:226-228) is a single `String.replace(DIRECTIVE_RE, '')` pass; the result is never re-scanned. Trace the input a note author can write inside a fence:

```mermaid
%%%{x}%%%{init: {"themeCSS": "…"}}%%
flowchart LR
  A-->B
```

Indices: 0=`%` 1=`%` 2=`%` 3=`{` 4=`x` 5=`}` 6=`%` 7=`%` 8=`%` 9=`{`…
DIRECTIVE_RE (`/%{2}{…/gi`) cannot start at index 0 (index 2 is `%`, not `{`), so the first match starts at index 1: `%{2}`=1,2; `{`=3; `(\w+)`=`x`; the optional body group matches empty because the `(?!}%{2})` lookahead sees `}%%`; `(?:}%{2})?`=5,6,7. The match is exactly `%%{x}%%` (1..7) and `lastIndex` becomes 8. From index 8 the remainder is `%{init: …}%%`, which has no `%%{` pair, so no second match occurs.

After the replace the surviving index-0 `%` is concatenated with index 8 onward, yielding `%%{init: {"themeCSS": "…"}}%%` — a syntactically valid mermaid init directive that `mermaid.render(id, …)` (mermaid.ts:468) then receives and `processDirectives`/`addDirective` honours.

Attack: any workspace collaborator or editor-role share-link visitor authors this fence; every other viewer of the note (including anonymous share-link visitors, shared-document.tsx:315) renders it. What lands in config is then gated only by mermaid's `secure` list (layer 1), which the module's own header comment (mermaid.ts:29-33) argues is insufficient because it pins only top-level keys — so a nested override that the strip was supposed to prevent from ever reaching the engine now reaches it. The correct fix is to loop the replace to a fixed point (or reject the fence outright when a `%%` sequence survives), not to rely on the pinned key list this layer was explicitly designed not to depend on.

verdict.reason: Code is exactly as described: stripConfigDirectives (mermaid.ts:226-228) is a single-pass replace with no re-scan or fixed-point loop, and its output is passed directly to mermaid.render (mermaid.ts:468) from a fully note-controlled fence body (mermaid.ts:371). I re-derived the regex trace against DIRECTIVE_RE (mermaid.ts:209-210) for the input '%%%{x}%%%{init:...}%%': the leftmost match cannot start at index 0 (index 2 is '%', not '{'), so it starts at index 1, and the optional body group matches empty because the (?!}%{2}) lookahead sees '}%%'; the match is exactly '%%{x}%%' (indices 1-7) with lastIndex 8, and the remainder '%{init:...}%%' contains no '%%'+'{' pair so it is left untouched. The surviving index-0 '%' then splices onto it, yielding a live '%%{init:...}%%' directive the engine reads. No guard elsewhere blocks this: nothing rejects a surviving '%%' or re-runs the strip, and the only remaining barrier is secure: SECURE_KEYS (mermaid.ts:438-443), which the module's own comments (mermaid.ts:29-33, 163-166, 213-217) state pins TOP-LEVEL keys only and which layer 2 was explicitly designed not to depend on, so nested overrides still land. In lane (unsafe handling of untrusted input in a bypassable sanitization layer on the one innerHTML path for note content rendered in other users' sessions, including anonymous share-link viewers) and blocking at major: a stated security layer is defeatable while reading as covered. Existing tests (preview.test.ts:560, 586) only exercise single well-formed directives, so nothing catches re-composition.

finding.summary: stripConfigDirectives() removes only the FIRST front-matter block, promoting a second `---`-delimited block to leading front matter that mermaid then parses as config — the strip creates a carrier that did not exist in the original source
finding.evidence:
`FRONTMATTER_RE` (mermaid.ts:211) is applied once, without the `g` flag, at mermaid.ts:227. Trace this note-authored fence body:

```
---
a: 1
---
---
config:
  themeCSS: "body{display:none}"
---
flowchart LR
  A-->B
```

`FRONTMATTER_RE` = `/^([^\S\n\r]*)-{3}\s*[\n\r](.*?)[\n\r]\1-{3}\s*[\n\r]+/s` with `\1` = ''. The lazy `(.*?)` first succeeds at `a: 1`, `[\n\r]`=`\n`, `-{3}`=`---`, `\s*`='' (it cannot take the following `\n` because `[\n\r]+` would then face `-`), `[\n\r]+`=`\n`. So exactly `---\na: 1\n---\n` is removed and the remainder passed to `mermaid.render()` (mermaid.ts:468) is:

`---\nconfig:\n  themeCSS: "body{display:none}"\n---\nflowchart LR\n  A-->B`

The strip therefore manufactures a config carrier rather than removing one, in the one function whose stated job (mermaid.ts:213-224) is that carriers 'never reach the engine' because `secure` pins only top-level keys.

Fix: strip front matter repeatedly until no leading block remains (or reject a fence whose body still starts with `---` after stripping).
